title: Load Balancing Algorithms
description: Explore the most common load balancing algorithms — round-robin, weighted, least-connections, IP hash, and the power of two random choices.

segments.text: Welcome back. Last time we saw why load balancing matters. Today, we're diving into the algorithms that decide which server gets each request. This is where the real engineering trade-offs live.

The simplest algorithm is round-robin. Request one goes to server A, request two to server B, request three to server C, then back to A. It cycles through servers in order, like dealing cards around a table.
Round-robin treats every server equally. But what if server A has 32 cores and server B has only 8? You're wasting capacity. That's where weighted round-robin comes in.
segments.thought_prompt: If server A is 4x more powerful, how many requests should it get compared to server B?

segments.text: With weighted round-robin, you assign weights proportional to capacity. Server A gets weight 4, server B gets weight 1. So A handles four requests for every one that B handles. Simple, but you have to set the weights manually.

Here's a smarter approach: least connections. Instead of guessing capacity, the load balancer tracks how many active connections each server has and sends new requests to whichever server is least busy right now.
Least connections adapts automatically. If one server slows down, its connections pile up, so it naturally gets fewer new requests. It's self-healing in a way that round-robin can never be.

Sometimes you need the same client to always reach the same server. IP hash solves this by hashing the client's IP address to pick a server. This gives you session affinity without storing session state in the load balancer.

The trade-off? If one server goes down, all clients pinned to it lose their sessions. And if traffic is unevenly distributed across IP ranges, your load becomes unbalanced. It's deterministic, but not always fair.

Now here's my favorite: the power of two random choices. Instead of checking all servers, you randomly pick just two and send the request to whichever has fewer connections. Surprisingly, this performs almost as well as checking every server.
segments.thought_prompt: Why would checking just 2 random servers be nearly as good as checking all of them?

segments.text: The math behind it is beautiful. With pure random selection, the most loaded server has O of log n over log log n requests. But with two random choices, it drops to O of log log n. That double-log improvement is massive at scale.

So which algorithm should you pick? Round-robin for homogeneous stateless services. Least connections when request durations vary. IP hash when you need sticky sessions. And power of two choices when you want great performance without centralized state.

The best algorithm depends on your workload, your infrastructure, and your consistency requirements. In the next lesson, we'll go deeper into L4 versus L7 load balancing and see how the layer you operate at changes everything.
